extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and educated readers/students of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on judging and creating poetry, focusing on the nature of poetic value, the relation of subject/form/substance, and how style and versification must fuse with meaning. Useful for critics and poets thinking about what makes a poem 'poetic.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's intrinsic value (Poetry for poetry's sake)
rubrics_metrics.description: “This experience is an end in itself, is worth having on its own account, has an intrinsic value.” Poetic value should be judged from within the poetic experience, not by external purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a poem primarily by the intrinsic imaginative experience it produces. External benefits (instruction, religion, culture, fame, moral effects) may be additional goods but cannot directly determine the poem's poetic worth. Examples/anti-patterns: treating a hymn's religious utility as evidence of poetic excellence (Lead kindly Light vs. a psalm paraphrase) conflates ulterior ends with poetic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid composing/valuing poetry for ulterior ends
rubrics_metrics.description: “The consideration of ulterior ends... tends to lower poetic value.” When poets compose with overt ulterior aims (didactic, propagandistic, commercial), the nature of poetry is changed and its poetic value is likely reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of making instruction, propaganda, or moral/political purpose the primary determinant of a poem's worth. Such motives can pull poetry out of its own atmosphere and result in diminished poetic experience. The guideline applies both to poets (in composition) and readers/critics (in evaluation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry must form an autonomous world requiring immersion
rubrics_metrics.description: “Poetry... to be a world by itself, independent, complete, autonomous; and to possess it fully you must enter that world, conform to its laws.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful poetry creates a self-contained imaginative world to which the reader must acclimate. Evaluate whether a poem establishes its internal laws and invites immersive contemplation rather than functioning merely as a reference to 'real' life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject (external topic) does not determine poetic value
rubrics_metrics.description: “The subject... is not, as such, inside the poem, but outside it... the poetic value cannot lie in that subject, but lies entirely in its opposite, the poem.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge a poem solely by its ostensible subject (title or topic). The same subject can yield poems of vastly different merit; value lies in how the poem treats and transforms its subject. Anti-pattern: assuming a grand subject (e.g., Fall of Man) guarantees greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject can provide aesthetic opportunity but is not decisive
rubrics_metrics.description: Some subjects (e.g., the Fall of Man) offer wider, more penetrating opportunities of poetic effect and may have some pre-poetic aesthetic value, but they do not determine eventual poetic quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that subjects vary in the scope of inchoate material they present; choose subjects aware of their affordances. Still, excellence depends on the poem's handling; a pin's-head subject can yield a great poem if transformed imaginatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and substance are inseparable in the poetic experience
rubrics_metrics.description: “When you are reading a poem... you do not experience separately... a certain meaning or substance, and... certain articulate sounds... you experience the one in the other... a resonant meaning.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poetry as an indivisible unity of sound and meaning. Analytical decompositions into isolated 'form' and 'substance' are products of reflection, not features of the poem itself. Critics should aim to re-create that unified poetic experience rather than treating components as independent scoring categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style must be truthful/adequate — words as equivalent symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: “The one virtue of style is truth or adequacy; that the word, phrase, sentence, should express perfectly the writer's perception, feeling, image, or thought; so that... the words are 'symbols equivalent with the thing symbolized.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose language that perfectly expresses the poet's perception or feeling. Beware paraphrase: replacing a line with an ostensibly 'equivalent' paraphrase often misrepresents the poetic stance (example: paraphrasing 'To be or not to be' loses the character's mode of being).

rubrics_metrics.name: Versification (sound, rhythm) must be expressive of meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: “The music is then the music of the meaning... the music is the music of the meaning, and the two are one.” Versification only truly matters when it is fused with and expressive of the poem's content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether meter, rhythm, and sonic features are integral to the poem's meaning rather than decorative musicality alone. Anti-pattern: valuing musical sound as an independent aesthetic to the exclusion of meaning—this yields limited pleasure and risks empty formalism. Examples: Virgil's line loses effect in prosaic translation because sound and meaning fuse there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mere decoration and conventional poetic diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Decorative effects or worn-out 'poetic diction' indicate a mixed or only partially poetic work; mere decoration cloaks preconceived matter rather than producing genuine poetic content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject surface ornamentation that dresses a preformed idea. If a passage is primarily decorative or a 'conceit' that does not yield new poetic content, the poem is less purely poetic. Wordsworth's critique of poetic diction is cited as an attempt to expose such worn-out phraseology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure poetry arises from an inchoate creative impulse
rubrics_metrics.description: “Pure poetry... springs from the creative impulse of a vague imaginative mass pressing for development and definition. If the poet already knew exactly what he meant to say, why should he write the poem?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value work in which meaning is discovered through composition rather than imposed beforehand. Composition should be a process of revelation where the poem's form and content emerge together; manufacture from a fully-formed idea tends to produce decoration rather than creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translations and paraphrases cannot fully preserve poetic meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A translation or paraphrase is a new product; changing words (or language) often changes meaning because meaning in poetry is bound up with particular words and their sounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating translations or paraphrases, recognize their inevitable limitations. Assess translations as distinct works and be cautious about claiming they reproduce the original poetic meaning; examples: Virgil and the effect of translating his line into prose lose essential poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical method: aim to re-create the poetic experience rather than decompose it
rubrics_metrics.description: “The true critic... is always aiming at a richer, truer, more intense repetition of that experience.” Analytical separation of form and substance is permissible but should be undertaken with the whole poetic experience in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should seek to repeat and illuminate the unified poetic experience for readers rather than reduce the poem to checklist components. Analytical discussion is useful, but remember that decomposed aspects are analytic products, not the poem itself; avoid treating such components as independent measures of value.
